messages.body_plain:

I humbly submit that I am not very sophisticated as yet with R, albeit I find the packages for CFA and IRT to be fantastic.  Thanks in advance if someone can help.

Robert Semel

messages.subject: Re: Standard errors of b estimates
messages.body_plain:
These can be computed via the delta method from coef(). See below for an example.

###
library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, SE=TRUE)
plot(mod, type = 'SE')
itemplot(mod, 1, type = 'SE')

coef(mod, printSE=TRUE)
coef(mod, IRTpars=TRUE, printSE=TRUE)
###

Phil

I am wondering if it is also possible to access the iteration history for the individual model parameters, or if anyone has any suggestions for how to do that?

Any suggestions related to this idea would also be appreciated! Thanks, Peter

messages.subject: Re: EM iteration history for individual model params?
messages.subject_clean: EM iteration history for individual model params?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

There's an undocumented 'storeEMhistory' options to the technical list which allows the EM history to be stored and extracted via extract.mirt(). See below

####
library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(Science, technical = list(storeEMhistory = TRUE))
extract.mirt(mod, 'EMhistory')
###

For the most part I don't see why users would necessarily need this as it mainly increases the size of the final object, but if the purpose is purely for pedagogy then I see no harm. HTH

Phil

messages.subject: Manually matching the MIRT log likelihood output
messages.subject_clean: Manually matching the MIRT log likelihood output
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone, I’m attempting to learn more about the log likelihood values that MIRT outputs in conjunction with its converged set of parameters. As part of this effort I’ve tried to match the  the log likelihood values that MIRT produces via manual calculation (using the final set of parameters from mirt). The results are close but don’t match. I’ve included a reprex below. My likelihood can’t accommodate missing data, but in my example, there isn’t any missing data so I expected the two numbers to be the same. Any ideas of where I might be going wrong here?

Thank you,

-Emre

reprex({
library(mirt)
library(data.table)

set.seed(1244)
n_items <- 100
n_people <- 10000
theta <- rnorm(n_people)
a <- runif(n_items, 0.5, 1.5)
b <- rnorm(n_items, 0, 1)
p <- matrix(0, n_people, n_items)
for (i in 1:n_people) {
    for (j in 1:n_items) {
        p[i,j] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-a[j]*(theta[i]-b[j])))
    }
}
response <- matrix(rbinom(n_people*n_items, 1, p), ncol=n_items) # simulate responses as a matrix

# estimate parameters with mirt -------------------------------------------

logLik_4PL_individual_fixed <- function(theta, a, b, c, u, response) {
  n_items <- length(a)
  logLik_individual <- numeric(n_people)
  for (i in 1:n_people) {
    theta_i <- theta[i]
    for (j in 1:n_items) {
      prob_ij <- ((c[j] + (u[j]-c[j]))* (1 / (1 + exp(-a[j]*(theta_i-b[j])))))
      if (response[i,j] == 1) {
        logLik_individual[i] <- logLik_individual[i] + log(prob_ij)
      } else {
        logLik_individual[i] <- logLik_individual[i] + log(1 - prob_ij)
      }
    }
  }
  return(sum(logLik_individual))
}

df <- copy(as.data.frame(response))
mod <- mirt(data = df, 1, itemtype = "2PL")
parms <- as.data.frame(coef(mod, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE))
mod@Fit$logLik
# [1] -569213.5 #MIRT loglik (I want to match this number.)
thetaEstimate <- fscores(mod)

# attempt to estimate loglik with logLik_4PL_individual_fixed func --------
# (logLik_4PL_individual_fixed is defined above)

#this version uses the "thetaEstimate" value created by the fscores() function
ll_val2 <- logLik_4PL_individual_fixed(theta = thetaEstimate, a = parms$items.a, b = parms$items.b,
                                       c = parms$items.g, u = parms$items.u,
                                       response = df)
ll_val2
# [1] -554790.5

#this version uses the "theta" values created by the rnorm() function that was used to simulate the data.
ll_val3 <- logLik_4PL_individual_fixed(theta = theta, a = parms$items.a, b = parms$items.b,
                                       c = parms$items.g, u = parms$items.u,
                                       response = df)
ll_val3
# [1] -554790.5  <- this is close, but it doesn't match the MIRT loglik.

})

messages.subject: Re: Manually matching the MIRT log likelihood output
messages.subject_clean: Manually matching the MIRT log likelihood output
messages.body_plain:
This is an estimate of the complete-data log-likehood, and assumes the theta parameters are fixed and known. mirt uses marginal ML as the criteria, so you'll need to perform numerical integration for each response vector over the theta distribution in order to match.

Phil

> > > > > > > # Iteration: 38, Log-Lik: -295725.121, Max-Change: #0.00010
> > > > > >
> > > > > > This is not a Rasch model. It's the graded response model (or 2PL if your data is dichotomous).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ab_3dim_rasch <- fscores(cmod)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Then I can get 3 theta values for each obj (student) in ab_3dim_rasch.
> > > > > > > F1 F2 F3
> > > > > > > 1 1.052343 2.150286 2.425081
> > > > > > > 2 1.052343 0.831582 1.111325
> > > > > > > 3 0.231678 0.823915 0.603081
> > > > > > > 4 0.385443 1.665016 0.524183
> > > > > > > 5 1.052343 1.590955 1.121802
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My qustion is: for obj1, since 1.052343<2.150286, can I say obj1 has a higher grade in F1 than in F2? I guess the answer is no, because I find that the values on each factor fit N(0,sigma).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I don't know what the N(0, sigma) means in this context. Each of these observations has a different SE and VCOV matrix computed from their respective posterior distribution. While you could make the test you want, you would have to save the associated VCOV matrices and perform a Wald test directly for each observation. BUT, this is rather sub-optimal, because the VCOVs aren't truly unbiased because they require assuming the estimated IRT parameters are fixed and known with 100% certainty.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have used the software Conquest and R package TAM, I can use command "constraints = cases" to set the mean of each latent dimension to zero, and if I don't want a 0 mean, I can write ""constraints = items".( If I understand correctly).  Is there a similiar argument for mirt? I have checked the package pdf but failed to find. Or do you know is there other packges or softwares that can work?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You could easily adjust the scale of the distribution to be exactly 0 for each column of factor scores, though I don't think that solves your problem or is at all interesting. What exactly are you trying to infer from your data? That will help us answer your questions better.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Phil
> > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks so much,
> > > > > > > Wang Ziming

messages.subject: Re: Theoretically observed response patterns
messages.body_plain:
Try the following, though be warned that if your test length is very long this can flood your RAM.

library(mirt)
x <- mirt(Science, 1)
full_table <- residuals(x, type = 'expfull')
head(full_table)

Phil
